title: Métis Governance, Leadership, and Elders
intro: Written community law, earned leadership, and living teachers. Questions 44-47 are answered in this lesson — your writing saves here.

terms.def: The comprehensive 1870 community laws of the Lac Ste. Anne, St. Albert, and St. Joachim Métis parishes, with enforcement, shaped with church leaders.
Someone followed for wisdom and action rather than elected office, such as crisis leaders like Gabriel Dumont and Louis Riel who emerged when communities were threatened.

body: As early as 1870 the Métis of three Alberta parishes held a comprehensive set of community laws with clear enforcement, shaped with Roman Catholic church leaders who mattered deeply to those communities. Rules reflected community values and priorities, governing life beyond the hunt.

Leadership was earned. Crisis leaders such as Gabriel Dumont and Louis Riel emerged when Métis communities were threatened, fighting without personal agenda, while Elders taught as living libraries: students who learn from Elders gain knowledge no book can give, which is why Aboriginal leaders often stand apart from non-Aboriginal office-holders.

The Laws of St. Albert show what earned order looked like on paper. By 1870 three Alberta parishes held a comprehensive code with enforcement behind it, shaped with church leaders who mattered to those communities. Rules reflected parish values and priorities, covering daily life far beyond the hunt, which is why the questions treat them as proof of government, not just custom.

Elders differ from office-holders in source of authority. An Elder is designated after acquiring significant wisdom, experience, and knowledge, and accepted by the community as its expert. Students who learn from Elders add living knowledge to book knowledge, and leaders formed this way answer to the people who recognize them rather than to an election cycle.

example.title: See it in the questions
example.text: Questions 44-47 ask for the St. Albert laws, how informal leaders emerge, what distinguishes Aboriginal leaders, and how students benefit from Elders. Answer each from the two paragraphs above.

check.prompt: What makes the Laws of St. Albert significant?
check.sample: Sample response: they show a complete Métis legal order by 1870, written community law with enforcement, reflecting parish values rather than imposed rule.

title: Different Historical Relationships: First Nations and Inuit
intro: Treaties for some, a different road for others. Questions 48-51 are answered in this lesson — your writing saves here.

terms.def: The ongoing nation-to-nation bond First Nations entered through historic treaties, carrying hunting, governance, and land understandings.
The route taken where no historic treaty was signed, as with the Inuit after 1960s resource interest, negotiated as comprehensive agreements.

body: Métis and Inuit relations with Ottawa differ from First Nations treaty relations because neither group signed a historic treaty with Canada. For First Nations, a treaty guarantee of hunting rights also meant maintaining the right to govern themselves, since hunt leaders were the government.

The Inuit faced no treaty push while the Arctic seemed remote. Interest arrived in the 1960s with resource exploration, and after forced relocations carried out without Inuit consultation, organized Inuit negotiators pursued land-claim agreements serving their people instead.

Notice the sequence, because the questions test it: remoteness first, then resource interest, then relocation without consultation, then political organization, then claims. Each step caused the next, and the Inuit road to agreements runs through modern comprehensive claims rather than historic treaties.

The comparison to hold is three-way. First Nations carry treaty relationships with hunting-and-governance understandings inside them. Métis carry scrip history and settlement-building outside the treaty frame. Inuit carry comprehensive-claim negotiations after mid-century disruption. Same Crown, three different legal roads.

example.title: See it in the questions
example.text: Questions 48-51 contrast the three relationships. Structure each answer as: the arrangement, what it preserved or cost, and one named piece of evidence.

check.prompt: Why did treaty hunting guarantees mean self-government to First Nations negotiators?
check.sample: Sample response: hunting parties were led by the same people who governed, so protecting the hunt protected traditional government itself.

title: Métis Experiences: Red River, Scrip, and Road Allowances
intro: Sorting, paper promises, and displaced communities. Questions 52-56 are answered in this lesson — your writing saves here.

terms.def: Paper certificates offered to Métis instead of treaty, redeemable for land or money. Fraud and speculation scattered families.
Displaced Métis who built makeshift homes on thin public road strips after being pushed off homesteaded land again and again.
The Red River Métis leader who defended Métis rights and nationhood in crisis.

body: Canada sorted Métis through scrip rather than treaty, and the system was a disaster: fraud, speculation, and pressure scattered close-knit families across a wide territory, making culture hard to preserve. The famous Red River leader of this resistance was Louis Riel.

Families pushed off homesteaded raw land when it was reallocated became squatters along road allowances, the thin public strips set aside for roads. Some Elders remember happy times there, so question 56 deserves an honest answer: community and culture persisted, but on land that was never secure. The 1991 Royal Commission findings on the Métis need the textbook's exact account, so answer question 55 with pages 55-60 open.

Scrip's mechanics explain the disaster. Certificates convertible to land or money invited fraud and speculation, and speculators harvested signatures while families scattered across a wide territory. Sorting people on paper destroyed the close-knit geography that culture needs, which is why the system counts as failure even where individual certificates paid out.

Red River is the counterpoint. There the Métis acted as an organized people with military capacity, elected hunt governance, and leaders who negotiated, which is why Riel's name anchors this lesson. Resistance with institutions behind it reads very differently from displacement without them.

example.title: See it in the questions
example.text: Questions 52-54 trace sorting, Riel, and scrip's failure as one chain. Write the chain as cause and effect: paper instead of treaty, speculation instead of settlement, displacement instead of home.

check.prompt: How did scrip create the Road Allowance People?
check.sample: Sample response: scrip gave paper instead of secure land, fraud and reallocation scattered families, and the displaced rebuilt as squatters on public road strips.
